title: Building three Unreal Engine prototypes in parallel with an AI swarm: architecture, workflow, and results | Epic Ai MegaJam
author: gryxitl
selftext:
For the Epic AI MegaJam, I tried building three game prototypes in parallel using AI agents, then played them to decide which one to finish.

The theme was Director’s Cut, so that selection process became my interpretation of it.

I never opened Unreal Editor myself during the jam. Which I think is really funny.

I directed the agents, worked on the infrastructure, reviewed their output and played the builds. The agents operated the editor through tooling and handled implementation, asset imports, builds and automated QA.

It allowed me to focus on game design itself and not minutiae.

# The game prototypes

# Feral Divinity

A Black & White-inspired god game with autonomous villagers, miracles and a creature to teach.

[Watch the gameplay video](https://youtu.be/fuk5Dd3E0TI)

# The Price of Power

An action RPG where gold pays for equipment, spells and bribing enemies into fighting for you.

[Watch the gameplay video](https://youtu.be/Xw958v5Yic0)

# SCRAPHEAP

A physics-driven vehicle combat game where you build a ridiculous cat battle car from salvaged parts, fight, repair and rebuild.

[Watch the gameplay video](https://youtu.be/7l2TO24tqOw)

I chose SCRAPHEAP because it consistently made me laugh while playing it. I spent the remaining time on its combat, building loop and presentation. Trying to smash bugs and adding glitter to the cars.

# The system architecture

The setup had four main pieces:

* A Mac running the swarm controller and Unreal Engine 5.8 editor instances.
* A Linux worker for remote builds and playtesting.
* A Linux inference server for supporting model calls and asset generation.
* An older ThinkPad that I used to direct everything remotely.

The swarm controller is [ShrimpHub](https://github.com/shrimplabs/shrimphub).

It's an autonomous development project/experiment I've been working on since early in the year.

It schedules agents against a self reorganizing task graph and coordinates the work across projects.

We started with eight concurrent agents and eventually raised the limit to twenty across the three games. That required provider fallbacks, better allocation between projects, and explicit checkout of shared editor instances.

Available compute wasn’t always the bottleneck. Sometimes an editor was sitting unused while an agent waited because the resource assignment wasn’t working properly. Normally this system works really well with Godot or other software that don't deal with binary assets and not gigantic editors. There was a lot to deal with in flight and I did a few test runs before the jam.

# The workflow

**1. Write a design document.**

I worked through the concepts with ChatGPT, then handed each design document to the swarm controller manager to break into a dependency graph. The initial plans contained about 210 tasks across the three games.

**2. Let the swarm work through the graph.**

Agents implemented tasks and ran checks through the available tooling. The queues grew as QA and more complicated tasks produced follow-up work. It took about 2 days for the swarm to crunch through all the tasks.

**3. Hand each project to a frontier agent for integration.**

This was an important step. Completing the task graph didn’t mean everything was connected into a playable game.

The handoff needed the original design document, the current state of the project and its remaining problems. Some design details had been lost when the initial tasks were created.

**4. Playtest, inspect and iterate.**

Claude Code used the Swarm Unreal QA tooling to interact with the games and capture screenshots. I played builds and made the calls about what felt good, what needed work and which game to choose.

**5. Generate and integrate assets.**

I had built a generative art pipeline that uses Trellis 2.0/Pixal3d and skintokens for making 3d models and rigging them. I also had image generation models for concepting and providing images to generate models from. I also ran local audio and sound generation models.

The agents still had to import, configure and debug those assets. Generated rigs and materials introduced their own problems.

# TL:DR

* Built three Unreal prototypes in four days with my existing swarm controller and up to twenty concurrent agents.
* I directed and playtested. Agents handled code, editor work, assets, builds and QA. I never opened Unreal Editor myself.
* The swarm took about two days. Connecting systems, cleaning up assets and making the games fun still needed hands-on direction.
* SCRAPHEAP made me giggle like an idiot when I buzzsawed another car, so it got the final push. Submitted for Windows, Mac and Linux. [Play it here](https://gryxitl.itch.io/scrapheap).

# How to try it

The two public tools are:

* [ShrimpHub](https://github.com/shrimplabs/shrimphub) — the swarm controller. (Now with 100% more unreal engine support)
* [shrimp-pi](https://github.com/shrimplabs/shrimp-pi) — lets a frontier agent delegate work to sub-agents using other model providers via Pi Agent instances.

The Unreal integration also used my existing `swarm_qa` plugin. The setup involved custom infrastructure, so those two repositories aren’t a complete one-click reproduction of the whole environment.

A manageable starting point would be one small Unreal prototype: get an agent able to build it, interact with it and capture a screenshot, then add task scheduling and concurrency once that loop works.
